clue.text: Recast gold ingots without returning to the digs

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the short word is read backwards
to recast metal is to melt it and pour it into a new shape, so the letters are remoulded
without means lacking, so the following letters are taken away from the fodder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone melts down gold bars somewhere other than their own rented rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: Take OT out of GOLDINGOTS to leave GOLDINGS, then rearrange to LODGINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Digs is informal British slang for rented rooms, the same thing as a lodger's accommodation.

clue.text: Food for pets necessary in the winter

definitions.meaning: first meaning: animal lungs, sold as offal for cats and dogs
second meaning: lamps, needed during the long dark evenings

explanation.surface: Pets need particular feeding through the cold months.
explanation.walkthrough: Lights are the lungs of a slaughtered animal, a traditional cheap pet food in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both offal lungs fed to animals and the lamps people switch on during dark winter evenings.

clue.text: Trade working hours for scarcity

indicators.note: working suggests something in motion, so the letters are set moving into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
H is the standard abbreviation for hours

explanation.surface: Commerce operating during business hours in a time of shortage.
explanation.definitionFit: A dearth is a lack or shortage of something, which is exactly what scarcity means.

clue.text: TV at one church is a source of coolness

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
CE is the Church of England
the box is slang for television

explanation.surface: A television in a church offers somewhere to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' means placed after here, so the TV piece comes last; 'box' is everyday slang for a television set.
explanation.definitionFit: An icebox is a chilled cabinet or refrigerator, something that keeps food cold.

clue.text: Where literary hacks eat?

parts.note: surface reading: a canteen or café favoured by writers
setter's reading: the name of the London street of hack writers also contains slang for food

explanation.walkthrough: Grub Street was a real London street where poor jobbing writers lived; grub is slang for food, hence the joke about eating.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a long-standing name for the world of needy, low-grade professional writers.

clue.text: Belief in article is minute

parts.note: the definite article
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for minute

explanation.surface: A faith described in a newspaper piece is tiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as tiny, but it is the unit of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Theism is a creed: conviction that a god or gods exist.

clue.text: Uncontrollable, lacking assistance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unable to stop oneself, as with laughter
second meaning: read literally as without help

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word into its parts, help plus less.
explanation.definitionFit: One is helpless with laughter when unable to stop, and helpless when nobody comes to aid one.

clue.text: Large tin may become essential

indicators.note: may become signals a transformation, so the letters turn into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A big can could turn out to be indispensable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something integral is a necessary part of a whole, fundamental and indispensable to it.

clue.text: Things are soaked in this boat centre and half dead

parts.note: a marina is a harbour for yachts and small craft

indicators.note: half asks for just one of the two halves of the following word to be kept

parts.note: the first two of four letters

explanation.surface: Things sit soaking in a harbour while someone is half dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A marinade is a seasoned liquid in which meat or fish is steeped before cooking.

clue.text: Old cricketer fellow at University left with elegance

parts.note: W. G. Grace, the famous Victorian cricketer
F is the abbreviation for fellow
U is the abbreviation for university
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A veteran cricketer and an academic colleague departed in style.
explanation.walkthrough: W. G. Grace was England's great nineteenth-century cricketer, the crossword's stock 'old cricketer'; cricket is a bat-and-ball game popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Graceful describes something done stylishly and smoothly, an adjective like the phrase.

clue.text: Player with no time for a bet

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so one letter is removed from the word that follows

parts.note: a flutter is a small wager in British slang
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A gambler too busy to place a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: A fluter is someone who plays the flute, a musical performer.

clue.text: Flier lost mitt by river

indicators.note: something lost is astray and disordered, so these letters wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the Ouse is a river in England

explanation.surface: An aviator mislaid a glove beside the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A titmouse is a small songbird, and any bird is something that flies.

clue.text: Large vessel's to continue to signal

parts.note: to flag is to signal, as when flagging down a taxi
to go on is to continue

explanation.surface: A big ship keeps on sending signals.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in reverse order in the clue; 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagon is a big bottle or jug for serving wine or ale.

clue.text: Tossed coin, then … er … (not clear)

indicators.note: something tossed is thrown about, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A speaker flips a coin and then trails off hesitantly.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots and 'er' mimic someone failing to make sense, which suits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Incoherent speech is muddled and hard to follow, lacking clarity of expression.

clue.text: A sum of money to act as umpire on what to put up for the best view

definitions.text: what to put up for the best view

parts.note: a grand is a thousand pounds or dollars
a cricket umpire is said to stand in a match

explanation.surface: Someone is paid a sum to referee where the spectators should be seated.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandstand is the main covered seating structure built at a sports ground to give spectators the best sight of play.

clue.text: At the interval, drinking place used by secretary?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the thing a typist uses

parts.note: a space is a gap or interval
a bar serves drinks

explanation.surface: During the theatre interval a secretary nips into the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: The long key along the bottom of a keyboard is pressed constantly by anyone typing letters.

clue.text: US building confined by a kind of column, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: pent, as in pent-up, means shut in
the agony column is the problem page of a newspaper

explanation.surface: An American building hemmed in by a classical pillar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' suggests architecture, but it is the newspaper agony column; drop its Y.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pentagon is the five-sided headquarters of the American Department of Defense near Washington.

clue.text: Fit satisfactorily into the joint

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mesh neatly with something
second meaning: an interlocking woodworking join with fan-shaped tenons

explanation.surface: Something slots neatly into a carpentry joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans that dovetail combine smoothly, and the carpenter's interlocking wedge-shaped join bears the same name.

clue.text: Men on phone (mobile)? A remarkable thing!

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so these letters move about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Men chatting on a mobile phone: what an amazing sight!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like the type of phone, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A phenomenon can be an extraordinary person or event, a marvel or wonder.

clue.text: Head with changes concerning stick

indicators.note: with changes says the word before it is altered, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A leader making alterations regarding a disciplinary stick.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling or stay firmly attached, as glue holds things together.

clue.text: Football officials drove up in top gear

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside another

parts.note: the FA is the Football Association, which runs English football

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: rode is a past tense of drive, as in driving a horse

explanation.surface: Football referees arrived in a car in fourth gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top gear' sounds like a car's highest gear, but it is clothing worn on top: a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A fedora is a soft felt hat, gear worn on the top of the head.

clue.text: Dull material used to fill up?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the filling food
definitions.meaning: second meaning: heavy starchy food that makes one feel full

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the second sense is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodge is both tedious, turgid prose and heavy filling food like suet pudding.

clue.text: Vessel for a man of the cloth?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small fast boat
second meaning: a tailor who cuts fabric

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of the cloth' usually means a clergyman; here it is literally someone who cuts cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutter is a single-masted sailing boat, and also the tailor who cuts out the pattern pieces.

clue.text: Produce a tie?

parts.note: surface reading: make a necktie
setter's reading: finish a race level with a rival, used as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated form is the verb: to finish exactly level with another competitor.
explanation.definitionFit: Racers who cross the line together leave the contest drawn, with no winner.

clue.text: Black moth: one found in old clothes

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
the eggar is a type of large brown moth

explanation.surface: A dark moth lurking in a wardrobe of old garments.
explanation.walkthrough: Moths suggest old clothes, but the definition is a person dressed in rags.
explanation.definitionFit: A beggar, poor and asking for alms, is traditionally pictured wearing ragged cast-offs.

clue.text: Kind of cattle crossing in this place?

parts.note: here means in this place
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: Cows crossing a road at this spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereford is a breed of red and white beef cow, named after the English county.

clue.text: Chafe part of leg after rubbing initially

indicators.note: after sends the leg part second, placing it behind the piece taken from the word that follows
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter
the joint above the foot

explanation.surface: A sore leg after something has rubbed against it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the leg part second, behind the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To rankle is to cause lasting irritation or resentment, figuratively to gall.

clue.text: Guidance giving cheap accommodation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the act of directing a vessel
second meaning: the lowest-priced passenger quarters on a ship

explanation.surface: Directions offered on where to stay on a budget.
explanation.definitionFit: Steering a vessel is directing its course, and the ship's cheapest third-class berths bear the same name.
